title.zh: 民主深化還是菁英變形記？印度農村選舉改革如何讓地方豪強「由暗轉明」
title.en: Democratic Deepening or Elite Persistence? How Electoral Reform Reshuffles Power in Rural India

summary.zh:
【總結】在發展中國家推行政治分權時，地方政權常被鄉紳豪強「俘虜」（elite capture），淪為少數人的私器。為了打破幕後黑手操縱、深化基層民主，許多國家嘗試改行行政首長直選，期盼藉由選民授權賦予村長真正的實權。加州大學柏克萊分校政治學者 Alyssa R. Heinze 針對印度馬哈拉施特拉邦的一場自然實驗展開深入調查，卻得出了一個發人深省的結論：直選確實大幅提升了村長的「實質權力」（de facto authority），但這並非因為弱勢群體翻身做主，而是傳統菁英改變了掌權策略——他們從原本隱身幕後、操控傀儡的「非正式俘虜」，轉向親自披掛上陣參選並掌控體制的「正式俘虜」。這項研究揭示了制度工程在面對盤根錯節的既得利益時所遭遇的嚴峻瓶頸。

【研究問題】長期以來，基層民主常因間接選舉而滋生「密室政治」。在傳統間接選舉體制下，村議會代表在神廟或廣場私下協商推舉村長，地方宗族頭人得以扶植聽話、缺乏政治資源的弱勢代議士作為傀儡（proxy），並透過強迫中途辭職輪流瓜分權力。國際政治學界與各國改革派因而寄望於「直選」，認為全民直選能打破既有利益集團的壟斷，選出具備獨立民意基礎與實質治理權威的首長。然而，在社會階層森嚴、資源極度不平等的全球南方農村，直選真能切斷菁英的控制網絡，還是僅僅重構了權力運作的微觀基礎？這是過去經驗研究罕見觸及的核心盲點。

【研究方法】本研究利用了印度馬哈拉施特拉邦（Maharashtra）極具說服力的準實驗（quasi-experiment）環境。該邦於 2017 年頒布改革，將村議會主席改為直選，又於 2020 年換屆後廢止，加之各村長達數十年的歷史性錯位選舉週期，使直選與間接選舉如同隨機分配。作者進行了長達兩年以上的質性田野調查，訪談逾 150 名官員、村長與村民，並精細對比結構特徵相似但選制不同的村莊。同時，研究團隊蒐集了 5 個地區共 604 個村議會的大規模調查數據（結合行為觀察指標與知覺指標）、數位化了 1,300 多個村莊的主席辭職行政檔案，最後對 2,347 名選民進行了預先註冊的情境實驗（survey vignette experiment），全方位驗證因果機制。

【結果】實證結果顯示，直選村長在會議發言時間、代表村莊對接上級官僚等實質權力指標上均顯著優於間接選舉村長。然而，村級政治並未因此平民化，反而是傳統高階種姓、地主階級在直選村長中的比例大幅上升。在間接選舉下，地方頭人透過逼迫傀儡辭職達成派系分贓；但在直選體制下，一旦首長離職必須重新舉行全村普選，瓜分權力的交易成本急劇攀升，逼得豪強無法再躲在幕後，只能倚仗財富、宗族動員與「肌肉力量」（暴力威懾）親自競逐首長寶座。這意味著直選確實消除了幕後黑手的「非正式干預」，代價卻是菁英徹底「正式接管」了國家機器。制度改革若缺乏強力的配額與再分配配套，往往只會讓特權階級換一套更合法的面具繼續統治。
summary.en:
**Summary:** Political decentralization in the Global South is frequently undermined by elite capture, leaving local executives subordinate to unelected, behind-the-scenes powerbrokers. To disrupt these entrenched patron-client networks, institutional reformers have long championed direct elections as a tool of democratic deepening that grants executives independent popular mandates. Exploiting an exceptional quasi-experiment in the Indian state of Maharashtra, Alyssa R. Heinze demonstrates that direct elections do indeed dramatically bolster the de facto political authority of village council presidents. However, this gain does not stem from subaltern empowerment or fractured elite coalitions. Instead, direct elections simply compel rural elites to shift their mode of control from informal manipulation via pliable proxies to formal capture—personally contesting and winning executive office to dominate political institutions from within.

**Problem:** In decentralized, highly unequal democracies, indirect elections often foster informal elite capture. Behind closed doors—frequently through village council meetings in temples—landed caste elites negotiate the rotation of political office, handpicking pliant, inexperienced proxy candidates who can be pressured to resign halfway through their terms. Although institutional theory posits that switching to direct elections will bypass these backroom bargains and empower autonomous leaders accountable to the broader electorate, little empirical work has examined how traditional oligarchs respond to such reforms in contexts of severe structural inequality. Does direct voting truly dismantle elite hegemony, or does it merely force powerful factions to innovate new strategies to preserve their dominance?

**Approach:** Heinze takes advantage of a unique institutional quasi-experiment in Maharashtra, where local council president elections were abruptly switched from indirect to direct in 2017 and reverted in 2020. Because centuries of administrative history have left village electoral cycles deeply staggered and asynchronous, councils were quasi-randomly exposed to direct or indirect rules. Heinze triangulates three rich sources of evidence: over two years of qualitative ethnography, including in-depth controlled case comparisons of villages and more than 150 elite interviews; original survey and behavioral data from 604 village councils across five large districts alongside a digitized administrative census of resignations from over 1,300 villages; and an out-of-sample, preregistered survey experiment with 2,347 voters to test the causal mechanisms linking formal elite capture to executive authority.

**Results:** The empirical findings show that directly elected presidents exhibit significantly higher de facto authority—measured by behavioral indicators such as floor time in official meetings and direct representation before state bureaucrats. Yet this authority arises because direct elections fundamentally alter the strategic calculus of traditional elites. Under indirect rules, elites prefer informal capture because dividing the executive term across multiple pliable proxies provides patronage and plausible deniability. Direct elections eliminate this divisibility, as any mid-term resignation triggers a costly village-wide election. Faced with acute uncertainty and principal-agent risks, wealthy, upper-caste elites abandon proxy governance and deploy their formidable wealth, networks, and physical intimidation to capture office directly. Heinze’s study underscores the enduring resilience of entrenched power: without binding structural counterweights, institutional engineering intended to bring power 'closer to the people' may merely legitimize elite rule.

keyArticle.title: Democratic Deepening or Elite Persistence? How Local Elites Adapt to Electoral Reform in Rural India
